diff --git a/docs/workload-id/troubleshoot-revoked-credentials.md b/docs/workload-id/troubleshoot-revoked-credentials.md
new file mode 100644
index 00000000000..a311a0a620f
--- /dev/null
+++ b/docs/workload-id/troubleshoot-revoked-credentials.md
@@ -0,0 +1,167 @@
+---
+title: Troubleshoot revoked application credentials
+description: Resolve revoked credential errors, inspect tokenRevocations, and determine whether Microsoft revoked an application credential.
+ms.topic: troubleshooting
+ms.date: 10/22/2026
+ai-usage: ai-generated
+# Customer intent: As an application owner or tenant administrator, I want to understand why an application credential was revoked and restore access safely.
+---
+
+# Troubleshoot revoked application credentials
+
+If an application can't acquire a token because its credential was revoked, the Microsoft Entra security token service (STS) can return one of these errors.
+
+| Error code | Error name | Error message |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| AADSTS700027 | `InvalidClientAssertionRevokedKeysProvided` | The provided client assertion for {X} is using a key which is revoked. Please specify a valid client assertion. |
+| AADSTS7005003 | `InvalidClientSecretRevokedKeysProvided` | The provided client secret keys for app '{X}' are revoked. Please specify a valid client secret. |
+| AADSTS7005004 | `InvalidClientAssertionRevokedKeysProvided` | The provided client assertion for {X} is using a key which is revoked. Please specify a valid client assertion. |
+| AADSTS7005005 | `FederatedIdentityCredentialRevoked` | The provided federated credential with id: '{Y}' for application '{X}' is revoked. |
+| AADSTS7005006 | `TokenRevocationBlocksIssuance` | {X} has blocked token issuance for this request. |
+
+In these messages, `{X}` is the application's application (client) ID, and `{Y}` is the federated identity credential ID. Match the message as well as the code: `AADSTS700027` can also indicate other client assertion validation failures.
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> A revoked credential error doesn't, by itself, mean Microsoft revoked the credential. Application owners and administrators with sufficient permissions can also revoke credentials. A populated `tokenRevocations` collection doesn't identify who performed the revocation either. Follow the checks in this article to determine the source.
+
+## Understand why a credential was revoked
+
+Microsoft can revoke a credential in your tenant after detecting that a threat actor compromised it. The threat actor might have stolen an existing credential or added a credential to an application or service principal to gain access.
+
+The `tokenRevocations` property records revocations on an application or service principal. Revoking a credential has the following effects:
+
+- The revoked credential can no longer be used as a client credential to acquire new tokens.
+- For some Microsoft resources, tokens already issued using the credential are invalidated before they expire.
+- For other resources, tokens already issued using the credential continue to work until they expire, which can take up to 24 hours. The revoked credential can't acquire a replacement token.
+
+Don't assume revocation immediately ends access to every resource. Investigate the compromise and the resources the application could access.
+
+## Check both the application and service principal
+
+Use Microsoft Graph to read `tokenRevocations` for both object types in the affected tenant. Your tenant might contain only the application object, only the service principal object, or both for the same application ID. A revocation can be recorded on either object. For background, see [Application and service principal objects](~/identity-platform/app-objects-and-service-principals.md).
+
+Use an account authorized to read the affected objects. The following requests use the Microsoft Graph `/beta` endpoint.
+
+1. Record the application (client) ID from the error and confirm which tenant the failed token request targeted.
+1. Replace `{appId}` with that application (client) ID, not an object ID. Query the application object's revocations:
+
+    ```http
+    GET https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/applications(appId='{appId}')/tokenRevocations
+    ```
+
+1. Query the service principal object's revocations with the same application ID:
+
+    ```http
+    GET https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/servicePrincipals(appId='{appId}')/tokenRevocations
+    ```
+
+1. Inspect both responses. Keep track of which object contains each revocation, even if you find a match in the first response.
+
+> [!TIP]
+> You can run these requests in [Graph Explorer](https://developer.microsoft.com/graph/graph-explorer). Sign in to the affected tenant with an authorized account; the unsigned-in sample tenant doesn't show your configuration. Select **GET** and **beta**, paste a request URL with `{appId}` replaced, and select **Run query**. The signed-in account needs appropriate access, and Graph Explorer needs consent for the required Microsoft Graph permissions. For help, see [Use Graph Explorer](/graph/graph-explorer/graph-explorer-overview).
+
+### Interpret the response
+
+A successful response contains a `value` array. A nonempty array means that the object has revocation entries. For example, this illustrative response shows a revoked client secret. Unrelated fields are omitted.
+
+```json
+{
+  "value": [
+    {
+      "@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.passwordCredentialRevocation",
+      "id": "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
+      "auditDetails": {
+        "reason": "Compromised credential",
+        "fromDateTime": "2026-10-22T12:00:00Z",
+        "issuedBy": "0e0fb671-b107-448b-a273-9d0ded7627a7"
+      },
+      "credential": {
+        "id": "aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee"
+      }
+    }
+  ]
+}
+```
+
+Inspect these fields for the revocation that affects your credential:
+
+| Field | What to look for |
+| --- | --- |
+| `id` | The revocation ID. Save this value if you need to delete the revocation. It isn't the application ID or credential ID. |
+| `credential.id` | The affected credential's ID. For a federated identity credential error, compare it with `{Y}` in the error message. |
+| `auditDetails.issuedBy` | The issuer's identifier. Use the check in the next section to determine whether Microsoft issued the revocation. |
+| `auditDetails.reason` | Optional free-text context about the revocation. The text can vary and isn't proof of who issued it. |
+| `auditDetails.fromDateTime` | The timestamp recorded in the revocation's audit details. Use it to help locate the corresponding audit event. |
+
+Handle other responses as follows:
+
+- An empty `"value": []` means that no revocations were returned for that object. Still check the other object type.
+- An object-not-found response can mean that the object type doesn't exist in your tenant. Confirm the tenant and application ID, and check the other object type.
+- An authorization error doesn't mean that no revocations exist. Resolve the access or consent issue before drawing a conclusion.
+- If the response includes `@odata.nextLink`, follow it to inspect the remaining entries.
+
+If neither object has a matching revocation, confirm the application ID, tenant, and credential used by the failing request. Don't attribute the failure to Microsoft without the evidence described next.
+
+## Determine whether Microsoft revoked the credential
+
+Either of the following checks confirms a Microsoft-initiated revocation. You don't need both to match.
+
+### Check the revocation issuer
+
+Inspect `auditDetails.issuedBy` on the matching revocation. If it equals the following value, Microsoft revoked the credential:
+
+```text
+0e0fb671-b107-448b-a273-9d0ded7627a7
+```
+
+The example response in the previous section contains this value. You can also use the audit logs to investigate the actor.
+
+### Check tenant audit logs
+
+Look for the update that recorded the revocation on the affected object:
+
+1. Sign in to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com) in the affected tenant as at least a [Reports Reader](~/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference.md#reports-reader).
+1. Browse to **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Audit logs**.
+1. Set the date range to include the revocation. Look for an **Update application** or **Update service principal** activity for the affected object.
+1. Open the event and review its target, changed properties, and initiator. A corresponding revocation update initiated by **Azure Active Directory Protection Services** means that Microsoft revoked the credential.
+
+Check that the event relates to the affected object and revocation, rather than an unrelated update. If you can't find the event, check the time range and your tenant's [audit log retention](~/identity/monitoring-health/reference-reports-data-retention.md). Missing audit history alone doesn't establish who revoked the credential.
+
+## Restore application access
+
+Investigate the credential and any unauthorized changes with your security team before restoring access. If Microsoft revoked it, treat the revocation as an indication that the credential was compromised.
+
+The recommended recovery is to replace the compromised credential and update the workload to use the replacement. Leave the compromised credential revoked, and remove credentials or access that a threat actor added. For application credential setup, see [Add and manage application credentials](~/identity-platform/how-to-add-credentials.md).
+
+### Remove a revocation
+
+If your investigation determines that the revocation was incorrect and the credential is safe to use, you can remove the revocation. You need permission to manage revocations on the affected object.
+
+> [!WARNING]
+> Deleting a revocation allows the credential to be used again if it's otherwise valid. It doesn't rotate the credential or remove a threat actor's copy of it. Don't remove a revocation from a compromised credential just to resolve the sign-in error.
+
+1. Save the revocation details for your investigation. Identify the object that contains the entry and the entry's top-level `id`.
+1. Replace `{appId}` with the application (client) ID and `{revocationId}` with that revocation ID. Use the request for the object that contains the entry.
+
+    For a revocation on the application object:
+
+    ```http
+    DELETE https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/applications(appId='{appId}')/tokenRevocations/{revocationId}
+    ```
+
+    For a revocation on the service principal object:
+
+    ```http
+    DELETE https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/servicePrincipals(appId='{appId}')/tokenRevocations/{revocationId}
+    ```
+
+    These requests don't require a request body. Delete only the entry you intend to remove; don't clear unrelated revocations.
+
+1. Repeat the earlier `GET` requests to confirm that the selected entry is gone and check for any remaining revocations affecting the credential. Deleting an entry from one object doesn't delete entries from the other.
+1. Retry token acquisition with the intended credential. If it still fails, review the new error and any remaining revocations.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Security best practices for application properties](~/identity-platform/security-best-practices-for-app-registration.md).
+- [Microsoft Entra audit logs](~/identity/monitoring-health/concept-audit-logs.md).
+- [Microsoft identity platform error codes](~/identity-platform/reference-error-codes.md).

englishSummary.headline: New guidance for troubleshooting revoked application credentials
englishSummary.summary: A new guide explains revoked-credential error codes, how to inspect tokenRevocations on applications and service principals using Microsoft Graph beta, and how to assess revocation effects and possible compromise.
englishSummary.adminImpact: Administrators can use the documented checks to diagnose token acquisition failures and determine whether revoked credentials may still allow access to some resources until existing tokens expire.

+ms.date: 10/18/2026

@@ -32,6 +32,10 @@ In the third scenario, Global Secure Access handles all Microsoft 365 traffic. N
 
 In the fourth scenario, Global Secure Access handles Internet and Microsoft 365 traffic. Netskope only captures Private application traffic.
 
+1. **[Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Microsoft Access with Netskope Internet Access](#microsoft-entra-private-access-and-microsoft-entra-microsoft-access-with-netskope-internet-access)**
+
+In the fifth scenario, Global Secure Access handles private application and Microsoft 365 traffic. Netskope only captures internet traffic.
+
 ## Prerequisites
 
 To configure Microsoft and Netskope for a unified SASE solution, start by setting up Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access. Next, configure Netskope Private Access and Internet Access. Finally, make sure to establish the required Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) and IP bypasses to ensure smooth integration between the two platforms.
@@ -73,6 +77,9 @@ Configure the `MSFT SSE M365` policy:
 - Repeat Steps 1 & 2 to Add Microsoft 365 IPs and save them as `MSFT SSE M365`:  
     `132.245.0.0/16`, `204.79.197.215/32`, `150.171.32.0/22`, `131.253.33.215/32`, `23.103.160.0/20`, `40.96.0.0/13`, `52.96.0.0/14`, `40.104.0.0/15`, `13.107.128.0/22`, `13.107.18.10/31`, `13.107.6.152/31`, `52.238.78.88/32`, `104.47.0.0/17`, `52.100.0.0/14`, `40.107.0.0/16`, `40.92.0.0/15`, `150.171.40.0/22`, `52.104.0.0/14`, `104.146.128.0/17`, `40.108.128.0/17`, `13.107.136.0/22`, `40.126.0.0/18`, `20.231.128.0/19`, `20.190.128.0/18`, `20.20.32.0/19`.
 
+> [!NOTE]

+

 ## Microsoft Entra Private Access with Netskope Internet Access
@@ -357,3 +364,65 @@ In the Netskope portal:
 1. Sign in to Netskope portal and browse to **Skope IT** > **Events & Alerts** > **Network Events**. Validate traffic related to the **RDP** session **is** present and that traffic related to Microsoft 365 and Internet Traffic such as Instagram.com, Outlook Online, and SharePoint Online is missing from Netskope Portal.
 1. In the system tray, right-click **Global Secure Access Client** and then select **Advanced Diagnostics**. In the network **traffic** dialog box, select **Stop collecting**.
 1. Scroll to observe that the Global Secure Access client **isn't** capturing traffic from the private application. Also, observe that the Global Secure Access client is capturing traffic for Microsoft 365 and other internet traffic.
+
+## Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Microsoft Access with Netskope Internet Access
+
+In this scenario, Global Secure Access handles private application and Microsoft 365 traffic. Netskope only captures internet traffic.
+
+### Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Microsoft Access configuration
+
+For this scenario:
+
+1. Enable the [Microsoft Entra Private Access forwarding profile](how-to-manage-private-access-profile.md) and the [Microsoft Entra Microsoft Access forwarding profile](how-to-manage-microsoft-profile.md#enable-the-microsoft-traffic-profile).
+1. Install and configure the Global Secure Access client for [Windows](how-to-install-windows-client.md) or [macOS](how-to-install-macos-client.md).
+
+### Netskope Internet Access configuration
+
+In the Netskope portal:
+
+1. Configure the `MSFT SSE Service` and `MSFT SSE M365` profiles, as described in [Netskope Location Profiles](#netskope-location-profiles), for use in the steering configuration.
+1. Set up a [Netskope steering configuration](https://docs.netskope.com/en/steering-configuration/) to steer web traffic.
+1. Install the Netskope client for [Windows](https://docs.netskope.com/en/netskope-client-for-windows) or [macOS](https://docs.netskope.com/en/netskope-client-for-macos).
+
+#### Add a steering configuration for internet access
+
+1. Navigate to **Netskope portal** > **Settings** > **Security Cloud Platform** > **Steering Configuration** > **New Configuration**.
+1. Enter a **Configuration Name**, such as `MSFTSSEWebTraffic`.
+1. Choose a **User Group** or **OU** to apply the configuration to.
+1. Under **Cloud, Web and Firewall**, select **Web Traffic**.
+1. Set **Bypass exception traffic at** to **Client**.
+1. Under **Private Apps**, select **None**.
+1. Under **Borderless SD-WAN Apps**, select **None**.
+1. Set **Status** to **Disabled** and select **Save**.
+1. Select the `MSFTSSEWebTraffic` configuration > **Exceptions** > **New Exception** > **Destination Locations**.
+1. Select `MSFT SSE Service` and `MSFT SSE M365`.
+1. Select **Bypass**, select the **Treat it like local IP address** checkbox, and then select **Add**.
+1. Select **New Exception** > **Domains** and add these domain exceptions: `*.globalsecureaccess.microsoft.com`, `*.auth.microsoft.com`, `*.msftidentity.com`, `*.msidentity.com`, `*.onmicrosoft.com`, `*.outlook.com`, `*.protection.outlook.com`, `*.sharepoint.com`, `*.sharepointonline.com`, `*.svc.ms`, `*.wns.windows.com`, `account.activedirectory.windowsazure.com`, `accounts.accesscontrol.windows.net`, `admin.onedrive.com`, `adminwebservice.microsoftonline.com`, `api.passwordreset.microsoftonline.com`, `autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com`, `becws.microsoftonline.com`, `ccs.login.microsoftonline.com`, `clientconfig.microsoftonline-p.net`, `companymanager.microsoftonline.com`, `device.login.microsoftonline.com`, `g.live.com`, `graph.microsoft.com`, `graph.windows.net`, `login-us.microsoftonline.com`, `login.microsoft.com`, `login.microsoftonline-p.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `login.windows.net`, `logincert.microsoftonline.com`, `loginex.microsoftonline.com`, `nexus.microsoftonline-p.com`, `officeclient.microsoft.com`, `oneclient.sfx.ms`, `outlook.cloud.microsoft`, `outlook.office.com`, `outlook.office365.com`, `passwordreset.microsoftonline.com`, `provisioningapi.microsoftonline.com`, `spoprod-a.akamaihd.net` > **Save**.
+1. Ensure that the `MSFTSSEWebTraffic` configuration is at the top of the list of steering configurations in your tenant. Then enable the configuration.
+1. Go to the system tray to check that Global Secure Access and Netskope clients are enabled.
+
+#### Verify configurations for clients
+
+1. Right-click **Global Secure Access Client** > **Advanced Diagnostics** > **Forwarding Profile** and verify that only Private Access and Microsoft 365 rules are applied to this client.
+1. Navigate to **Advanced Diagnostics** > **Health Check** and verify that no checks fail.
+1. Right-click **Netskope Client** > **Configuration**. Verify that **Steering Configuration** matches the name of the configuration you created. If not, select the **Update** link.
+    > [!NOTE]
+    > To troubleshoot health check failures, see [Troubleshoot the Global Secure Access client](troubleshoot-global-secure-access-client-diagnostics-health-check.md).
+
+#### Test traffic flow
+
+1. In the system tray, right-click **Global Secure Access Client** and then select **Advanced Diagnostics**. Select the **Traffic** tab and select **Start collecting**.
+1. In a browser, access `bing.com`, `salesforce.com`, and `yelp.com`.
+1. In the system tray, right-click **Global Secure Access Client**, select **Advanced Diagnostics**, and then select the **Traffic** tab.
+1. Scroll to confirm that the Global Secure Access client **isn't** capturing traffic from these websites.
+1. Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center and browse to **Global Secure Access** > **Monitor** > **Traffic logs**. Verify that traffic to these websites **isn't** recorded in the Global Secure Access traffic logs.
+1. Sign in to the Netskope portal and browse to **Skope IT** > **Events & Alerts** > **Page Events**. Verify that traffic to these websites **is** recorded in the Netskope logs.
+1. Access a private application you configured in Microsoft Entra Private Access. For example, open an RDP session to a private server.
+1. Sign in to Microsoft Entra admin center and browse to **Global Secure Access** > **Monitor** > **Traffic logs**.
+1. Verify that traffic for the RDP session **is** recorded in the Global Secure Access traffic logs.
+1. Sign in to the Netskope portal and browse to **Skope IT** > **Events & Alerts** > **Network Events**. Verify that traffic for the RDP session **isn't** recorded.
+1. Access Outlook Online (`outlook.com`, `outlook.office.com`, `outlook.office365.com`) and SharePoint Online (`<yourtenantdomain>.sharepoint.com`).
+1. In the system tray, right-click **Global Secure Access Client** and then select **Advanced Diagnostics**. In the **Traffic** dialog box, select **Stop collecting**.
+1. Scroll to confirm that the Global Secure Access client handled the Microsoft 365 traffic.
+1. To verify that the traffic is recorded in the Global Secure Access traffic logs, navigate to **Global Secure Access** > **Monitor** > **Traffic logs** in the Microsoft Entra admin center.
+1. In the Netskope portal, browse to **Skope IT** > **Events & Alerts** > **Page Events**. Verify that traffic to Outlook Online and SharePoint Online **isn't** recorded.

messageCenterItems.title: Microsoft Entra: Choose your own telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication
messageCenterItems.summary: Starting October 30, 2026, Microsoft Entra ID allows organizations to choose a supported third-party telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication via Microsoft Security Store. Microsoft-provided SMS/voice authentication retires by February 1, 2027, except for some users until July 1, 2027. Organizations manage provider relationships directly.
messageCenterItems.body:
What and why

Starting October 30, 2026, Microsoft Entra ID will make Choose Your Own Telephony Provider (CYOT) generally available. CYOT enables organizations to use a supported third-party telecommunications provider for SMS and voice authentication. Organizations select a supported provider through Microsoft Security Store and manage their commercial relationship directly with the provider.

Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys, instead of SMS or voice authentication. Organizations should use a telephony provider only for user populations that have a business, regulatory, or technical requirement for telephony-based authentication. 

Rollout schedule

  • General Availability (Worldwide): Beginning October 30, 2026

Impact on your organization

Who is affected

  • Organizations with users who require SMS or voice authentication for business, regulatory, or technical reasons

Platforms and services

  • Microsoft Entra ID
  • Microsoft Security Store

What will happen

  • Starting October 30, 2026, organizations can choose to configure a supported telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication.
  • Your selected provider will deliver the SMS messages or voice calls users need to complete authentication.
  • Microsoft Entra ID will continue to enforce authentication method policies and coordinate the authentication experience.
  • Your organization will manage its commercial relationship with the selected provider.
  • Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication is scheduled to be retired on February 1, 2027, for all users except Global Administrators and external users. The retirement date for Global Administrators and external users is July 1, 2027. Internal guest users remain subject to the February 1, 2027 retirement date.
  • After the applicable retirement date, users whose only available MFA method is SMS or voice must register a passkey during sign-in unless the organization has configured a supported telephony provider. This registration prompt is blocking.

Action required and recommendations

If your organization plans to adopt CYOT:

  • Identify affected users. Determine which users have a documented business, regulatory, or technical requirement for SMS or voice authentication.
  • Evaluate phishing-resistant alternatives. Confirm that a phishing-resistant authentication method does not meet the requirements for those users.
  • Review supported telephony providers. Compare providers based on geographic coverage, supported delivery channels, pricing, support, security, and compliance capabilities.
  • Review organizational requirements. Work with the appropriate teams to review procurement, privacy, and regulatory requirements before selecting a provider.
  • Plan your transition. Review Passkeys by default and retirement of Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication and plan your transition based on the retirement date applicable to each user population.
  • Validate purchasing requirements. Review Purchase a SaaS solution and deploy a linked solution. Purchasing through Security Store requires an Azure billing subscription and resource group, plus the appropriate Azure subscription role.
  • Estimate costs. Review provider pricing and expected Azure infrastructure charges before deployment.

Learn more

  • Choose a telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication - Microsoft Entra ID | Microsoft Learn
  • Estimate telephony provider and Azure hosting costs: ExternalPhoneProvider-AzureFunction-Sample/docs/COST-CALCULATOR.md at main · Azure-Samples/ExternalPhoneProvider-AzureFunction-Sample
  • Passkeys by default and retirement of Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication - Microsoft Entra ID | Microsoft Learn
  • Purchase and deploy a SaaS solution from Security Store - Microsoft Security Store | Microsoft Learn

Compliance considerations

QuestionAnswer
Does the change add any integration to third-party software products, and if so, what?Yes. The change enables organizations to use a supported third-party telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication. Organizations select a provider through Microsoft Security Store, and the selected provider delivers the SMS messages or voice calls used for authentication.
